title: Bleak outlook for shares as RBA ponders move
full_text:
The outlook for Australian shares just became worse – you can add the risk of more interest rate rises by the Reserve Bank to the list of reasons for the S&P/ASX 200 to underperform over the next 12 months.
For the past few years, Australia’s benchmark index has significantly lagged the booming US market.
A much larger exposure to the artificial-intelligence boom has driven US performance well ahead of Australia’s. This year the S&P 500 is up 12 per cent, versus a 3.7 per cent gain for the ASX 200, despite a mini-boom in commodities. But what if the RBA is forced to start lifting rates again?
So far the ASX 200 has pretty much shrugged off the RBA’s three rate rises earlier this year.
A 12-month forward PE of about 18 times is little changed from January. However, the index fell as much as 1.1 per cent on Thursday – its biggest one-day fall in three months – before closing down 1 per cent at 9038.2 points, as rate expectations spiked after Wednesday’s inflation surprise.
Within hours of the July CPI data showing inflation is already reaccelerating well above RBA forecasts for the September quarter, Deutsche Bank, NAB and Citi predicted another rate rise in September, while Goldman Sachs and CBA called for an RBA increase in November.
UBS chief economist George Tharenou said the risk of an “early” rate rise in September had “increased materially” after the household spending indicator beat expectations significantly again.
The market-implied chance of a September rate rise soared to almost 50 per cent. A November increase was fully priced, with a 50 per cent chance of a further move by February.
But does the stockmarket now fully reflect the risk of more rate rises and a hard landing?
Bloomberg’s surveyed “recession probability” until recently was just 20 per cent – even lower than in the US. Surely that number is way too low, even if none are forecasting a recession.
On the charts, a fall below 9000 could spark a fall to the 200-day moving average near 8800.
Morgan Stanley equity strategist Chris Nicol says the stockmarket had leaned on a comfortable assumption.
“The common pushback to our generally more cautious views linked to an equity investor belief that the next move in rates would be down,” he said.
That belief was boosted after a soft June CPI reading sparked a rally in rate-sensitive stocks. But the July inflation rebound tells a different story.
Nicol says the strong rebound in inflation aligns with “clear evidence from this results season of cost push pressure and business-to-business and business-to-consumer pricing intentions.” “A need to hike by the RBA is not in the current market make-up,” Nicol warns. In his view, the current slowdown “could rise in impact and magnitude”, yet Australian banks are trading on elevated PE multiples around 18 times and the consumer discretionary sector on 23 times, levels that are “not reflecting the risk of further rate hikes”.
On one side, the sharemarket is thriving. The ASX 200 is not far off record highs. About two-thirds of stocks are above their 200-day moving average – the most in about a year. “The sharemarket doesn’t seem to care,” Global X senior investment strategist Marc Jocum says.
But for households, the picture is certainly murkier. Annual underlying inflation was stuck at 3.6 per cent last month, with fuel soaring 7.5 per cent and rents up 0.4 per cent.
That leaves the RBA with what Jocum calls “some serious scar tissue”. Having already cut rates by 75 basis points this year only to see inflation reaccelerate, he thinks the bank will be wary of declaring victory too soon. “The dilemma is whether the RBA reacts to noisy monthly data or waits for the quarterly inflation print in November,” he says.
Yet consumers keep spending. Household spending rose 1.1 per cent in July and is up 7 per cent over the year, the strongest pace since June 2023.
Global X’s Jocum also flags a deeper problem.
Real GDP per capita has fallen to one of the weakest rates in the modern era under the Albanese government. “We’re effectively putting more people into the factory without making the factory more productive, and that is an economic problem interest rates simply cannot solve,” he says.
Property adds to the confusion, with prices falling and buyers unsure whether to move. “Australians increasingly don’t know what to do,” Jocum says. “Buy, sell or wait? Fix or float? Spend or save?” Even so, he notes record inflows into ETFs, suggesting investors are finding ways to navigate the uncertainty even as the broader economic path stays unclear. His final message is a warning to policymakers: “The sharemarket can climb a wall of worry, but households need confidence that the ground beneath them won’t keep shifting. Confusion is an economic tax, and Australia cannot afford to keep paying it.”
